title: A needle's eye (Song of Songs Rabbah 5:2)
hookLine: open for Me an opening like a needle's eye, and I'll open for you like a great hall
tomorrow: and if even that feels too far, who walks the rest of the way?

cards: The text you didn't answer last week. The friend you meant to call back a month ago. The longer it sits, the bigger the reply seems to need to be, until it's so big you never send it at all.

Silence turns into a wall, one day at a time, and nobody ever decided to build it. A midrash on the Song of Songs speaks straight to that feeling, and answers yesterday's teaser with the smallest opening there is.

teach.b: The verse is a lover at the door, knocking at night: "Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled." The rabbis read the Song as a love story between God and Israel, so here God is the one knocking.

And Song of Songs Rabbah has the Holy One say: my children, open for Me one opening of teshuvah, of return, as small as the eye of a needle, and I will open for you openings wide enough for wagons and carriages to pass through.
God's part: a gate for traffic.

teach.h: TOO LATE TO START SMALL? NO.
teach.b: The midrash makes the first move almost absurdly small. Not a speech. Not fixing everything.
A pinprick of light. And notice that God doesn't ask Israel to open the door all the way, only to stop holding it completely shut.
Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: in this midrash, the tiniest hole in the world is enough for God to work with. Now bring it to this week.

For a quiet friendship, a needle's eye might be two words: thinking of you. For a practice you dropped, one blessing, one line. For someone who has drifted from God, maybe just standing at the door and not walking away.
The midrash takes away one excuse in particular: that it's too late to start small.

how: Jewish teaching on teshuvah, return, stresses that it can begin at any time and with a small step; this midrash is often taught in the season before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.

o: a narrow gate in an old city wall at night
a test that only very humble people can pass
the tiny opening God asks for, to open a huge one

p: as small as a needle's eye
wide enough for wagons and carriages
God knocking, in the rabbis' reading

s: in this midrash, coming back after a long time needs a big gesture first
an opening the size of a needle's eye is enough.
the rabbis read the Song of Songs as a love story between God and Israel
so the one knocking at the door is God.
in the verse, Israel is the one knocking at God's door
the voice at the door says: open to me.

games.q: you used to say a blessing before meals, then stopped for months. starting again feels like it'd need a whole new routine. by the midrash, what's the move?
o: wait until you can restart properly, with a full daily routine.
admit the moment has passed; it's too late to just start again.
say one blessing before one meal today, and let it open from there.
games.why: a needle's eye is all the midrash asks of you; God promises to open the rest wide enough for wagons.

practice: Find a scrap of paper and a pen. Write the smallest possible first message to someone, or something, you've let go quiet: five words or fewer. Look at how tiny it is, then fold it and keep it where your hand will find it later.

wordCard.voice: A needle's eye: Song of Songs Rabbah's picture of return. Open an opening as small as a needle's eye, and God opens one wide enough for wagons.

orig.note: Hebrew: an opening, a doorway. the midrash's word for both the needle-sized opening and the wide one.

carryVoice: Your line: a needle's eye. That's all the opening the midrash asks of you; the wagons are someone else's job.

sources.ref: Song of Songs Rabbah 5:2 (open for Me an opening of repentance like the eye of a needle, and I will open for you openings through which wagons and carriages can pass)
